name: Bahal Temple
significance: Three red-brick Vajrayana Buddhist sanctuaries standing about 500 m apart on the Padang Lawas plain, and the only temples of that scattered complex to have been fully restored. Archaeologists place their construction between the 11th and 13th centuries and link them to the Pannai kingdom, a trading polity inside the Srivijayan sphere.

name: Maha Vihara Maitreya
significance: A modern Mahayana complex covering 4.5 hectares in the Cemara Asri estate at Medan, built from 1991 by the Indonesian Buddhist association and inaugurated in 2008. Its three worship halls seat between 1,500 and 2,500 people each, and it is described as the largest modern Buddhist temple in Indonesia.

name: Banyunibo Temple
significance: A single-cella Buddhist candi in the valley south of the Ratu Boko plateau, unusual among surviving Central Javanese Buddhist temples for a curved roof crowned by one solitary stupa. Discovered collapsed in 1940 and reconstructed by 1978, it carries Kala-Makara ornament, Bodhisattva and Tara figures in its niches, and reliefs of Hariti and Vaisravana.

name: Jabung Temple
deity: Buddhist mortuary shrine of Bhre Gundal of Majapahit
style: Red-brick East Javanese candi, octagonal body with stupa roof
significance: A tall red-brick Majapahit sanctuary dated by a carved doorframe block to 1276 Saka, or 1354 CE. The Pararaton records it as the mortuary temple of the royal Bhre Gundal, and the Nagarakretagama names it Bajrajinaparamitapura, visited by King Hayam Wuruk on his tour of East Java in 1359.

name: Jawi Temple
style: East Javanese candi with cube-and-stupa pinnacle
significance: A slender 24.5 m temple raised as the mortuary shrine of Kertanegara, the last king of Singhasari, and built to express the Shiva-Buddha synthesis he professed: a Shaivite cella holding a yoni, with Durga, Ganesha, Nandi and Brahma images, set beneath a pinnacle combining a cube with a Buddhist stupa.
story: When lightning struck the monument in 1331 the image of the Buddha Akshobhya is said to have vanished from it, a disappearance read as a manifestation of shunyata, emptiness.

name: Merak Temple
significance: A Shaivite temple in Klaten with a main shrine and three ancillary perwara chapels, assigned to the Mataram kingdom of the 9th or 10th century on the evidence of its yoni and its Ganesha and Durga Mahishasuramardini images. Reconstruction of the 1,480 sq m compound was completed in 2011, and its stairway carries unusual makara-naga chimeras.

name: Bubrah Temple
deity: Buddha (guardian shrine of the southern direction in the Manjusrigrha mandala)
style: Buddhist candi within a mandala plan
significance: A 9th-century Buddhist candi between Sewu and Prambanan that served as the southern direction-guardian shrine of the great Manjusrigrha mandala centred on Sewu. Its Javanese name means broken or disorderly, earned by centuries in ruins; a reconstruction costing 11 billion rupiah ran from 2011 and was inaugurated in December 2017.

name: Sojiwan Temple
significance: A Mahayana Buddhist temple south of Prambanan, dated by the Rukam inscription to between 842 and 850 and understood as a dedication to Queen Pramodhawardhani, whose name the site carries. Its main shrine rises 27 m and its base is carved with bas-reliefs illustrating Pancatantra and Jataka fables; reconstruction, delayed by the 2006 earthquake, finished in December 2011.

name: Gunung Wukir Temple (Canggal)
significance: The earliest structure attributed to the ancient Mataram kingdom, a Shaivite compound of one main shrine and three perwara with a Nandi and a yoni pedestal. The Canggal inscription found here in 1879 records King Sanjaya ordering a lingam raised in 654 Saka, 732 CE, which fixes both the temple and the kingdom's beginning.

name: Kimpulan Temple
significance: A small, plainly decorated Shaivite shrine near Yogyakarta holding a lingam-yoni with Ganesha and Nandi images, its chambers probably once roofed in wood in the manner of Balinese meru. It came to light by accident on 11 December 2009 during excavation for a university library, buried some five metres deep under Merapi ash like Sambisari, Morangan and Kedulan.

name: Badut Temple
significance: Reckoned the oldest temple in East Java, a Shaivite shrine whose garbhagriha holds a lingam and yoni and whose outer niche carries Durga Mahishasuramardini. The Dinoyo inscription places it in 682 Saka, 760 CE, under King Gajayana of Kanjuruhan, and it keeps the older Central Javanese temple form despite its East Javanese setting.

name: Gebang Temple
deity: Ganesha (with a yoni in the inner chamber)
significance: A compact 8th-century Hindu shrine on a 5.25 m square base, holding a yoni in its cella and a Ganesha seated on a spouted yoni on its west side, with niches for Nandiswara. Buried under Merapi lahar deposits, it was found in 1936 and rebuilt by Van Romondt between 1937 and 1939; its roof figures peering from window frames echo the Bima temple at Dieng.

name: Sari Temple
significance: A two-storey Buddhist building beside Candi Kalasan, raised under the same Kalasan inscription of 778 that ordered a sanctuary for the bodhisattva Tara and a vihara for monks; scholars read Sari as that monastic dwelling. Its walls carry 36 Buddhist figures in tribhanga pose along with Tara, bodhisattva and kinnara reliefs, once coated in the protective vajralepa plaster.

name: Pura Penataran Sasih
significance: The former state temple of the Pejeng kingdom, dated by a chronogram at its entrance to 1266 and holding a tall stone seat for Ganesha in the main courtyard along with Hindu sculpture of the 10th to 12th centuries. It is best known as the home of the Moon of Pejeng, a colossal early bronze kettledrum kept in the temple.

name: Rimbi Temple
deity: Parvati (as the deified Queen Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi)
style: Andesite East Javanese candi on a brick foundation
significance: A Shaivite Majapahit temple in the Jombang hills raised in memory of Queen Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, whose portrait statue took the form of Parvati. About 12 m of the andesite structure survives on a three-tiered base, carrying 51 reliefs on themes of water and purification; it was noted by Alfred Russel Wallace and listed as a Cultural Property of Indonesia in 2020.

name: Ijo Temple
deity: Shiva (linga and yoni), with three perwara for the Trimurti
significance: The highest-set of the temples around Prambanan, standing at about 410 m on a hill some 4 km from Ratu Boko. Its main shrine holds a large linga and yoni wreathed by a naga, read as the union of Shiva and Parvati, while three smaller perwara facing east honour the Trimurti of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.

name: Kedulan Temple
significance: A Shaivite compound of one east-facing main shrine and three ancillary temples, with a lingga-yoni in the cella and images of Durga Mahishasuramardini, Nandiswara, Mahakala, Ganesha and Agastya; associated inscriptions date it to about 869. Sand miners struck it by accident on 24 November 1993 some six metres below the modern surface, where Merapi lava flows had buried it, and restoration has run in stages since 2017.

name: Ngawen Temple
deity: The five Dhyani Buddhas (a Ratnasambhava image survives in the north shrine)
significance: A row of five andesite Buddhist shrines near Muntilan, thought from the detail of their carving to be slightly older than Borobudur and understood as a dedication to the five Dhyani Buddhas; the north temple keeps a headless meditating Ratnasambhava in varamudra. Rampant lion figures at the corners and ratna pinnacles more usual on Hindu temples mark the group out.

name: Surawana Temple
deity: Memorial shrine of Wijayarajasa, Prince of Wengker
significance: A modest west-facing Majapahit temple built in 1390 and dedicated in 1400, at the shraddha rite for Wijayarajasa, Prince of Wengker and an uncle by marriage of King Rajasanagara. Only the reconstructed base stands intact, but it carries dense reliefs of the Arjunawiwaha, Sri Tanjung and Babuksha tales together with naga, makara and gana figures.

name: Lumbung Temple
significance: A 9th-century Buddhist group a few hundred metres north of Prambanan, laid out like Sewu with one main shrine ringed by sixteen stupa-crowned perwara. Its original name is lost; the nearby Kelurak inscription naming a compound dedicated to the bodhisattva Manjusri is generally taken to refer to Sewu rather than to this temple.
